name: Bright Purple
lede: Bright purple is a plain descriptive name for a vivid, saturated purple; it is a color of the synthetic age, because Ball reports that painters still had no pure, bright purple in the eighteenth century.

sections.title: A descriptive name
sections.body: Bright Purple is not a historical color name with a traditional story [1]. It is a modifier plus a basic color word, so the books use the phrase in its ordinary sense and never define it as a named shade [1][2]. The swatch here is a very saturated blue-leaning purple, close to [[violet]] and [[indigo]] in hue and far more intense than the dusty [[mauve]]. It is a screen color, and no pigment or dye is claimed to match it [3].

sections.title: Before synthetic dyes
sections.body:
Ball notes that, as of the eighteenth century, there were still no pure and bright purples on the painter's palette, and greens were a particular problem too [1]. Ball counts greens among the other persistent problems of the palette [1].

The change came with coal-tar chemistry. Perkin's 1856 experiment gave, in St Clair's telling, a bright purple liquid that dyed silk and held its color in light [4]. Ball sums up the new industry as one that turned out bright purples, lustrous reds, shocking pinks and brilliant yellows [5]. Greenfield adds a social reaction: in 1860s London the critic Hippolyte Taine, seeing women in bright purple gloves, took the loud colors as a sign of a parvenue or worse, though the women were respectable [6].

sections.title: Two older appearances
sections.body: Newton is reported by Ball to have blended dry pigments, among them orpiment, a bright purple, a light green and a blue, and seen an impression of brilliant whiteness from a few paces away [7]. Gage describes a painting in which bright purples and greens in the draperies were mixed with black, in the near absence of blue [8]. In both cases the words are the authors' description of a color, not the name of a pigment [7][8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive tools could not compute a reliable match count for this swatch, so no painting statistics are quoted here [3]. It sits at the loud end of the purple family, which is why it reads on screens as an electric purple rather than a natural one [3].

questions.q: Why were pure bright purples scarce in painting before the 1850s?
choices: Painters had to mix them from red and blue, which dulls them
Purple pigments were poisonous to use
The word purple did not exist
questions.answer: Painters had to mix them from red and blue, which dulls them

questions.q: Bright Purple is the name of a historic dye with a recorded origin story.

openers: Painters had no pure bright purple until coal-tar dyes arrived in the 1850s.

issues: lede overstated 'dyers' and 1850s; limited to Ball's eighteenth-century painters' palette
